client: I've been really stressed out lately because my business is not doing as well as I expected, and then last week I got hit with these unexpected tax bills that I honestly didn't see coming at all. The financial pressure just feels like it's crushing me from all sides, and I keep lying awake at night running the numbers in my head over and over. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because at the end of the day the bills are still going to be there no matter what I say in here.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — the business stress, the surprise tax bills, the sleepless nights — and it makes complete sense that you'd feel crushed and even skeptical that talking could help when the practical problems are still sitting there. You're right that our conversations won't make the bills disappear, but what we *can* work on is the relentless mental loop that's keeping you up at night, because that cycle of worry often makes the situation feel even more unmanageable than it actually is. I'm curious — when you're lying awake running those numbers, what's the worst-case thought that tends to show up most often?

client: The worst-case thought is that I'm going to lose everything — like, the business completely fails, I can't pay the tax bill, and then I end up losing my apartment too because I've been dipping into personal savings to keep things afloat. It sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but at 2am it feels completely inevitable, not just possible. And then I start thinking about how I'd have to explain that to my family, and that's almost worse than the financial part itself.
therapist: It doesn't sound dramatic at all — that fear of losing everything and then having to face your family with it carries a really deep kind of pain, almost like the shame feels heavier than the practical crisis itself. What's worth noticing is what you said: at 2am it feels *inevitable*, not just possible — and that shift from "this could happen" to "this will definitely happen" is exactly where our minds can betray us under stress. Can you tell me a little about what the actual current evidence looks like — are there any signs that things are still recoverable, even if they're hard to see right now?

client: I mean, I guess if I'm being honest, the business is still open and I do still have some clients — it's not like revenue has gone to zero. And I managed to get a payment plan set up with the tax office, so it's not like they're going to show up and seize anything tomorrow. But here's the thing — even when I try to remind myself of those facts during the day, by the time 2am rolls around it's like that evidence just evaporates and the catastrophic version takes over completely, so I'm not sure how useful it is to list the positives if my brain just ignores them when it matters most.
therapist: You've actually just identified something really important — the evidence *is* there (the business is still running, you have clients, you have a payment plan), but at 2am your brain essentially goes offline for rational thinking, which is a completely real neurological thing that happens when we're exhausted and anxious, not a personal failure. So the goal isn't just to *have* the evidence, it's to build a response that can reach you even in that vulnerable 2am state — things like a written note to yourself, a grounding routine, or even a specific phrase you've pre-decided to trust. What does that 2am moment actually look like for you — do you stay in bed, get up, reach for your phone — what's the pattern?

client: Honestly, I reach for my phone almost immediately — I start doing these frantic calculations on the calculator app, or I'll open my banking app and just stare at the numbers like somehow they're going to change. I know it makes things worse but it feels like I'm at least doing something rather than just lying there feeling helpless. The written note idea sounds a bit too simple to me, like I'm not sure a few words on paper are really going to compete with that level of panic.
therapist: What you're describing makes a lot of sense — grabbing the phone feels like taking control, but what it's actually doing is feeding the panic with more ammunition at the exact moment your brain is least equipped to process it calmly, so it becomes this exhausting loop. You're right that a simple note probably can't compete with that level of urgency, which is why I'd actually suggest the goal isn't to *calm* the panic with words, but to *interrupt* the phone ritual with something that gives your hands and mind something else to do — because right now the phone has become the anxiety's best friend. What do you think is really driving that urge to check — is it more about trying to solve something, or is it about not being able to tolerate the uncertainty of just not knowing?

client: Honestly, I think it's more about the uncertainty — like if I just check one more time, maybe I'll find some number that finally makes me feel like things are okay, but that number never comes. It's like I'm searching for a feeling of safety that the phone just can't actually give me, which I can kind of see logically but can't seem to stop doing. I guess what worries me about interrupting that ritual is that I don't know what I'd replace it with that would feel even remotely as satisfying, because at least the checking feels like I'm engaged with the problem rather than just surrendering to it.
therapist: You've just described something really profound — you're not actually looking for information when you check your phone, you're looking for *relief*, and that's a crucial distinction because no number will ever be emotionally satisfying enough to quiet that need. The good news is that what you're really after — a sense of safety and being okay — is something we can actually work on building through other means, and "replacing" the ritual doesn't have to mean surrendering to helplessness; it can mean finding something that engages you just as actively but doesn't pour fuel on the fire. What does feeling genuinely calm or safe feel like for you in other areas of your life — are there moments, even small ones, where you've felt that without needing to solve anything?

client: There are moments, I think — like sometimes when I'm cooking something that requires actual concentration, I notice I'm not thinking about the business at all, or occasionally if I'm watching something genuinely engaging on TV. But those feel almost accidental, like I can't manufacture that state on purpose, and I worry that if I tried to deliberately do those things at 2am it would feel forced and hollow compared to the urgency I'm feeling. I guess I'm also a bit skeptical that something like cooking or watching TV is really in the same league as this level of financial panic.
therapist: What's really interesting is that you've already discovered something important about your own brain — it *can* let go of the panic when it's genuinely absorbed in something else, which means the capacity for relief is already in you, even if it feels accidental right now. You're right that cooking at 2am might feel strange, but what you're describing isn't really about the activity itself — it's about deliberately choosing to *not* give the anxiety what it's demanding, which is actually a powerful act rather than a passive one. I'm wondering — when you imagine trying one of those absorbing activities at 2am instead of reaching for your phone, what feels like the biggest obstacle: the practical side of it, or something more like a feeling that you don't *deserve* to feel calm until the problem is solved?

client: That last part actually hit me harder than I expected — the idea that I don't deserve to feel calm until it's solved. I think there's something real in that, like some part of me believes that if I relax even for a moment I'm being irresponsible, or that I'm not taking the situation seriously enough. It feels almost like the anxiety is proof that I care about fixing it, and letting go of it even temporarily would be some kind of betrayal of how serious things are.
therapist: That's a really courageous thing to notice about yourself — this belief that anxiety equals responsibility, and that calm equals not caring, is incredibly common but also incredibly costly, because it means you've essentially made suffering a *moral duty*. The painful irony is that the exhausted, panicked version of you staring at a banking app at 2am is actually far less capable of solving this problem than a you who has genuinely rested and recovered, so the anxiety isn't protecting the business — it's quietly working against it. I'd gently invite you to consider: if a close friend came to you with this exact situation and said they felt guilty for taking a break, what would you tell them?

client: I'd obviously tell a friend that rest isn't the same as giving up, and that burning yourself out doesn't actually fix anything. But when I try to apply that to myself it just feels different, like the logic works for other people but somehow my situation is a special exception where I really do need to keep suffering to stay on top of it. I can hear how irrational that sounds even as I'm saying it, but knowing it's irrational doesn't seem to make it feel any less true.
therapist: The fact that you can hear the irrationality and still feel it just as strongly is actually one of the most honest and important things you can recognize — it tells us that this isn't a knowledge problem, it's a deeply held belief about yourself that logic alone can't touch, almost like part of you feels you're uniquely undeserving of the compassion you'd freely give anyone else. That "special exception" feeling is worth really sitting with, because it often has roots that go beyond this current crisis — like it might be connected to older beliefs about what you have to *do* or *suffer* to be worthy or responsible. I'm curious — does this feeling that you need to keep suffering to prove you care show up in other areas of your life too, or does it feel specific to this financial situation?

client: Honestly, now that you're asking, I think it does show up elsewhere — like I have a really hard time taking a day off even when the business is doing fine, and I always feel vaguely guilty if I'm enjoying myself when there's anything unresolved on my plate. But I'm a little nervous about going too far down that road, because it starts to feel like we're moving away from the actual financial crisis that I need to deal with right now. I don't want to spend our time unpacking my whole childhood when there are real bills sitting on my kitchen table.
therapist: That's a really fair and grounding thing to say, and I want to honour it — you're not here to get lost in the past, and the bills are real and need attention. But what you've just described isn't really a detour from the financial crisis — it's actually the engine behind the 2am phone checking, the inability to rest, and the belief that suffering equals responsibility, all of which are making the crisis harder to navigate right now. So we don't need to unpack your whole history, but gently understanding *why* your mind fights rest so hard could be the most practical thing we do — because it's directly affecting your ability to think clearly about those bills. What would feel like the right balance to you — staying focused on the practical coping strategies while keeping an eye on this deeper pattern when it shows up?

client: That framing actually makes sense to me — I don't want to ignore the pattern completely if it's genuinely making things worse, but I also need to feel like we're keeping the financial stress as the main focus rather than it becoming a footnote. I think the balance I'd want is something like, if that deeper belief shows up and it's directly getting in the way of me coping with the bills, then we look at it, but we don't go digging for it. The thing I'm still not sure about is whether understanding why I do this will actually change anything in the moment, or if I'll just have more self-awareness while still reaching for my phone at 2am anyway.
therapist: That balance you've described is really wise and we can absolutely work that way — the deeper pattern stays in service of the practical problem, not the other way around. And your skepticism about insight versus actual change is completely valid, because you're right that understanding alone rarely rewires a habit in the heat of the moment — which is why alongside the "why," we also need to build a very concrete, almost mechanical plan for that 2am moment that doesn't rely on you being your wisest self when you're exhausted and panicked. So I'd love to work with you on something specific — a short, realistic sequence of actions to try instead of reaching for the phone, designed around what we already know works for you, like that absorbing-activity piece. Would you be open to mapping that out together today, so you have something tangible to actually test this week?
